html:
On 16 October 1905 the viceroy Lord Curzon split the province of Bengal in two. The protest that followed, the Swadeshi movement, was the first mass campaign against British rule.

Bengal had 78 million people and was hard to govern as one unit. The new province of Eastern Bengal and Assam, with its capital at Dhaka, had a Muslim majority. The west, joined with Bihar and Orissa, left Bengali speakers a minority in their own province. Officials wrote in private that a united Bengal was a power and a divided one would pull in different ways. Calcutta's educated Hindus, the heart of the national movement, saw the aim clearly.

On the day itself people fasted, bathed in the Ganges and tied threads on each other's wrists as a sign of unity, an idea of Tagore, who wrote songs for the cause. The movement's weapon was swadeshi, "of our own country": boycott British cloth, sugar and salt and buy Indian. Foreign cloth was burnt in the streets. Indian mills, banks and schools were started, among them Tata Steel. Some young men turned to bombs.

Many Muslims favoured the new province, and the Muslim League was founded at Dhaka in 1906.

The partition was cancelled in 1911, and the capital of India moved to Delhi. Bengal was divided again in 1947.
sum: On 16 October 1905 the viceroy Lord Curzon split the province of Bengal in two. The protest that followed, the Swadeshi movement, was the first mass campaign against British rule.
